University of Nairobi, PO Box 30197, Nairobi, Kenya Received 1978 December 1; in original form 1978 April 18 Summary. This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of the lower Proterozoic granites, exposed in the western part of Kenya and dated at 2530 k 50 Ma (ARb = 1.39 x lO-"yr-'). Ten sites out of 13 have yielded stable palaeo- magnetic directions which are believed to be primary. Polished section and thermomagnetic analyses indicate titanomagnetite grains as the main carrier of the primary component of the natural remanence. The mean palaeo- magnetic north pole is calculated at 2 10.7" E, 60.9" N with Ag5 = 13.5".

Douglas Peninsula Formation The Douglas Peninsula Formation, the lowest formation of the Pethei Group, occurs throughout the aulacogen and varies in thickness from 16-33 m (Hoffman 1968). The type section was sampled. It is 25 m thick and it is autochthonous (Hoffman er al. 1977). The rock is a thin-bedded, fissile, red marlstone, that is composed of small lenticles of pink or brown limestone in dark reddish-brown mudstone. The dominant opaque mineral is haematite, which occurs as a dusting on sedimentary grains, and as very fine blebs on sand grain boundaries. Three axial plane traces were observed in the folds of these rocks and suggest three phases of deformation and metamorphic activity in them. A number of indi- vidual flows and feeder dykes were identified and successive flows were separated by a 3-5 m thick redbole horizon suggesting that there were significant time intervals between their eruptions. Magnetic anisotropy Other possible causes of paleomagnetic variation are the effects of magnetic anisotropy. The magnetization of the Matachewan dykes could be deflected either as a result of intrinsic anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility of the diabase (Stacey 1960), or from shape anisotropy related to the tabular nature of dyke bodies (Abrahamsen 1986). In the first instance, anisotropy may arise from flow patterns in the dyke such that the maximum susceptibility axis lies within the dyke plane parallel to paleoflow, and the minimum axis is perpendicular to the dyke.

In the first instance, anisotropy may arise from flow patterns in the dyke such that the maximum susceptibility axis lies within the dyke plane parallel to paleoflow, and the minimum axis is perpendicular to the dyke.

Abstract- Results of a palaeomagnetic study carried out on the Migori granites exposed in the South Western part of Kenya are presented. The granites of Post-Nyanzian and Post- Kaviron- dian ages are dated at 2739 5:111 Ma and 2420 5:60 Ma, respectively, using the whole rock Rb- Sr isochron method. Alternating frequency and thermal demagnetization techniques have been used to isolate characteristic components of natural remanence. Opaque petrological and thermomagnetic studies indicate titanomagnetite grains as the main carrier of the primary component. The 2505 Ma Ptarmigan swarm consists of only a few dykes (Fig. 1). These brown-weathering, north- to northeast- trending dykes, up to 45 m wide, are characterized by coarse clinopyroxene (25%), orthopyroxene (20%), and olivine (5%) in a matrix of calcic plagioclase (45%) and accessory Fe–Ti oxides, biotite, and apatite. They are generally fresh with minor uralitic amphibole after pyroxene, chlorite, ser - pentine, and magnetite after olivine, and sparse serpentine and chlorite-filled veinlets.

CONCLUSIONS Paleomagnetic sampling in the Siwalik Group of Nepal presents a number of challenges. In this paper we present several refinements and im- provements over previous studies. Detailed paleo- magnetic sampling and analysis demonstrate that paleosols and sandstones, even where very fine grained, do not yield reliable paleomagnetic directions, whereas laminated siltstone yields ex- cellent results. Thermal demagnetization behavior and field tests of paleomagnetic stability suggest that the ChRM is primary or near primary. The correlation of our magnetic polarity zonation with the geomagnetic polarity timescale of Cande and Kent (1995)

This observation suggests complete sampling of geomagnetic secular variation and indicates that the time interval of NRM acquisition was short compared with the few thousands of years of dominant periodicities of secular variation. Tauxe and Kent (1984) provided strong arguments that the NRM of similar sedimentary rocks in the Siwalik Group of Pakistan was a depositional remanent magnetism carried by hematite and was acquired essentially at the time of deposition.

8C O N C L U S I O N S A palaeomagnetic study of igneous and sedimentary rocks from central Massachusetts produces several Early to Middle Jurassic pole positions that con rm the J1 cusp and sub- stantiate a high-latitude Middle Jurassic pole. The Early Jurassic pre-J1-cusp pole positions are carried by a within-plate type of tholeiite, the Holden diabases, and lacustrine sediments at the Triassic Jurassic boundary. The lacustrine mudstones have a high-coercivity component with peak unblocking tem- peratures of 660u C, and a shallow normal polarity with north- easterly direction, interpreted as a primary direction carried by early haematite.

Conclusions (1) The MVT mineralisation in the M-JC district has a primary chemical remanent magnetisation as its ChRM that is carried by both pyrrhotite and magnetite and that resides in both dolomite and sphalerite. The magnetisation is coeval with MVT mineralisation, post-dates brecciation, and post-dates most or all tilt deformation. The MVT mineralisation is paleomag- netically dated at 316 F 8 Ma, and is interpreted to have been emplaced after the peak of Alleghanian orogenesis in the M-JC district.

The Nankoweap Formation is a 113 – 250-m-thick sequence consisting entirely of hematite-cemented sandstones (Elston and Scott, 1976) . The Nankoweap Formation was first identified and described by Va n Gundy (1934, 1951) , but was not formally classified and isolated as a formation until the mapping of Maxson (1961) . This red bed sequence is unconform- ably bound below by the Unkar Group and above by the Chuar Group. The exact genetic relationship of the Nankoweap to older and younger GCSG strata remains poorly understood (Timmons et al., 2001) .

Susceptibility versus temperature measurements show that the predominant magnetic mineral in the Frere Formation from DDH #1 and DDH #2 is hematite but a small amount of magnetite also is present in some specimens. However, numerous spec- imens displayed clear evidence for the production of magnetite between 300 and 500 ◦C by alteration of a weakly magnetic phase. Specimens from the Penarth and Lias groups have similar NRM intensities to those from the Blue Anchor Formation, but because they are dominantly from micritic silty limestones, they show the lowest susceptibilities. Hysteresis measurements (up to 1 T) indicate that the non-red lithologies are dominated by a paramagnetic behaviour (consistent with magnetic torque measurements of Hounslow, 1985 ), whereas the red mudstones have, in addition, a nonsaturating high coercivity ( N100mT) component, consistent with haematite being present.

review_quotes.text: Specimens from the Penarth and Lias groups have similar NRM intensities to those from the Blue Anchor Formation, but because they are dominantly from micritic silty limestones, they show the lowest susceptibilities. Hysteresis measurements (up to 1 T) indicate that the non-red lithologies are dominated by a paramagnetic behaviour (consistent with magnetic torque measurements of Hounslow, 1985 ), whereas the red mudstones have, in addition, a nonsaturating high coercivity ( N100mT) component, consistent with haematite being present.

In conclusion, the mineralogical studies indicate that the magnetisation of red mudstones in the Twyning Mudstone Formation is dominantly carried by haematite (in some cases with goethite), with both reversed and normal polarities. The Blue Anchor Formation and the Penarth and Lias groups are dominated by a magnetite-like phase, which again carries both polarities. There is weak evidence, from the three-component IRM, that a magnetic sulphide may be important in some Lias Group samples, and possibly also in some from the Penarth Group. This magnetic sulphide may be partly responsible for the stronger Brunhes-age overprint in those samples.

4 ROCK MAGNETIC RESULTS Strong-ﬁeld thermomagnetic experiments (Figs 3a and b) for the samples of Paomagang and Wangdian areas suggest a predominance of haematite as the magnetic carrier. Curie temperatures around 685 ◦C are observed, both on heating and cooling. IRM acquisi- tion curves (Figs 3c and d) show that no saturation is achieved up to the maximum ﬁeld of 2.7T, indicating the dominance of high- coercivity minerals, such as haematite or/and goethite. The pres- ence of haematite is indicated by thermal demagnetization of the composite IRMs, while goethite is not clearly visible in the curves (Figs 3e and f).

The HTC was unblocked in a range between 400 ◦C and 690◦C, indicating haematite as a remanence carrier. The HTC is isolated from 34 out of 42 sites. Erratic demagnetization behaviour precluded an identiﬁcation of remanent directions in the remaining eight sites (one site of the Paomagang area and seven sites of the Wangdian area).

Thermal demagnetization isolated two components in most samples. A low unblocking tem- perature component ( <350 ◦C) that does not decay to the origin is interpreted as a drilling induced magnetization. The second, high temperature component (HTC), isolated at tempera- tures >400 ◦C, unblocks univectorially towards the origin. The HTC passes the McFadden-fold test with an overall mean tilt-corrected direction of Dec = 255◦, Inc =− 24◦ (N = 7, α95 = 9◦). As in the basaltic samples, the LTC is oriented moderately down to the north, whereas the ChRM in these samples is sub-horizontal and directed toward the east. The genesis of the hard hematite ore deposits at Ely and Soudan on the Vermilion Range, Minnesota, U.S.A. (Fig. 1) has been disputed. Winchell and Winchell (1891) proposed that they are anamorphosed primary chemical sediments. Clements (1903) and Abbott (1907) proposed that iron-bearing groundwater solutions metasomatically replaced the primary iron-formation in structural troughs. Van Hise and Leith (1911) argued that groundwater leached and oxidized the primary iron-formation to form residual soft hematite deposits, which at Soudan were metamorphosed directly to hard hematite and at Ely were weathered to laterites and then metamorphosed. Our preliminary microscopic observations of the Mugford basalts indicate that the magnetic material present is magnetite occurring sparsely in polished sections. It is fine grained (typical grain-size is 20 x 20 p) and is present as in- clusions in pyroxenes. Exsolution or zoning were not observed. In some places magnetite is altered to leucoxene, and chlorite and epidote are also observed. However, there is no evidence from these sections that the bulk of the mae- " netite, which most probably is the carrier of the observed stable magnetism, is of secondary origin.
